q: Carter Little 2007 Justifying knowledge, justifying method, taking action: epistemologies, methodologies, and methods in qualitative research
why: The clearest published statement of how epistemology, methodology and method nest — the backbone of tab A1.

q: Johnson Onwuegbuzie 2004 Mixed methods research: a research paradigm whose time has come Educational Researcher
why: Defines mixed-methods research and its pragmatist rationale; useful if your design combines a survey with interviews or FGDs.

q: Morgan 2007 Paradigms lost and pragmatism regained methodological implications of combining qualitative and quantitative methods
why: Explains paradigms in plain terms and argues for pragmatism as the working philosophy of applied research.
How design-based identification changed empirical economics; read before writing your model-specification justification.
The standard survey of programme-evaluation estimators (matching, DiD, IV, RD) with their identifying assumptions.
The practitioner's guide to regression discontinuity — what to report and how to defend an RD design.

q: Kiel McClain 1995 House prices during siting decision stages: the case of an incinerator from rumor through operation
why: Source of the pooled cross-section incinerator example used in tab C2 (year81 × nearinc).

q: Williams 2006 Generalized ordered logit/partial proportional odds models for ordinal dependent variables Stata Journal
why: Methodological justification for the partial proportional odds model used in the RQ–method table example.
Why transparent, reproducible data handling (do-files, raw vs clean data) is now expected in economics.

q: Stevens 1946 On the theory of scales of measurement Science
why: The original nominal–ordinal–interval–ratio typology and the statistics each level permits.

q: Jamieson 2004 Likert scales: how to (ab)use them Medical Education
why: A short, much-cited warning about treating Likert items as interval data.

q: Carifio Perla 2008 Resolving the 50-year debate around using and misusing Likert scales Medical Education
why: The reply to Jamieson: distinguishes Likert items from Likert scales and defends parametric analysis of summated scales.
Shows parametric methods are robust with Likert data — the key reference when you run OLS on a scale score.
Two-page practical guide to analysing and reporting Likert-type data.
Experimental evidence on how many response categories agree–disagree scales should have.

q: Preston Colman 2000 Optimal number of response categories in rating scales: reliability, validity, discriminating power, and respondent preferences
why: Compares 2- to 11-point and 101-point rating scales on reliability, validity and respondent preference.

q: Liddell Kruschke 2018 Analyzing ordinal data with metric models: what could possibly go wrong
why: Shows when treating ordinal outcomes as metric produces wrong conclusions — the case for ordered models.
The original sample-size table discussed in tab D4; read it with Lakens (2022).

q: Cohen 1992 A power primer Psychological Bulletin
why: Defines small/medium/large effect sizes and gives sample sizes for 80% power across common tests.
The G*Power 3 paper — cite it when you report an a priori power analysis.
Power analysis for correlation and regression in G*Power 3.1 (the f² approach used in tab D4).
The best modern guide to justifying a sample size: precision, power, resource constraints and heuristics.

q: Green 1991 How many subjects does it take to do a regression analysis Multivariate Behavioral Research
why: Origin of the N ≥ 50 + 8m rule of thumb — and why power analysis does better.

q: Peduzzi Concato Kemper Holford Feinstein 1996 A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression analysis
why: The events-per-variable guideline for logit models with a binary outcome.

q: Ioannidis Stanley Doucouliagos 2017 The power of bias in economics research Economic Journal
why: Finds most economics studies are underpowered — the economics case for power analysis.

q: McKenzie 2012 Beyond baseline and follow-up: the case for more T in experiments Journal of Development Economics
why: Power and sample-size planning for field experiments with repeated rounds of data.

q: Biernacki Waldorf 1981 Snowball sampling: problems and techniques of chain referral sampling
why: The methodological classic on snowball sampling of hidden populations.

q: Heckathorn 1997 Respondent-driven sampling: a new approach to the study of hidden populations Social Problems
why: How respondent-driven sampling improves on snowball sampling for hard-to-reach groups.

q: Palinkas Horwitz Green Wisdom Duan Hoagwood 2015 Purposeful sampling for qualitative data collection and analysis in mixed method implementation research
why: Typology of purposive sampling strategies and when each fits.

q: Baker Brick Bates Battaglia Couper Dever Gile Tourangeau 2013 Summary report of the AAPOR task force on non-probability sampling
why: Authoritative review of what can and cannot be inferred from non-probability samples, including online panels.

q: Groves 2006 Nonresponse rates and nonresponse bias in household surveys Public Opinion Quarterly
why: Why a high response rate does not guarantee low nonresponse bias.

q: Krosnick 1999 Survey research Annual Review of Psychology
why: Evidence-based review of question wording, response options, acquiescence and satisficing.

q: Stantcheva 2023 How to run surveys: a guide to creating your own identifying variation and revealing the invisible Annual Review of Economics
why: Survey design written by and for economists: sampling, question design, attention checks, experiments in surveys.

q: Bertrand Mullainathan 2001 Do people mean what they say? Implications for subjective survey data American Economic Review
why: When subjective survey answers can and cannot be used as variables in economics.
Rising nonresponse and measurement error in the big household surveys economists rely on.

q: Beatty Willis 2007 Research synthesis: the practice of cognitive interviewing Public Opinion Quarterly
why: How to pretest questionnaire items with cognitive interviews before the pilot.

q: Brislin 1970 Back-translation for cross-cultural research Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology
why: The back-translation procedure for English–Malay (or other) questionnaire versions.

q: Beaton Bombardier Guillemin Ferraz 2000 Guidelines for the process of cross-cultural adaptation of self-report measures Spine
why: Step-by-step protocol for adapting an established instrument to a new language and culture.
How economists measure financial literacy (the 'Big Three' questions) — an example of an adopted instrument.

q: Hinkin 1998 A brief tutorial on the development of measures for use in survey questionnaires Organizational Research Methods
why: Step-by-step scale development: item generation, content validity, factor analysis, reliability.
A nine-step primer for developing and validating scales — the practical workflow behind tab E4.

q: Podsakoff MacKenzie Lee Podsakoff 2003 Common method biases in behavioral research: a critical review of the literature and recommended remedies
why: Common-method bias in single-source surveys and the procedural remedies to build into your questionnaire.

q: Cronbach 1951 Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests Psychometrika
why: The original coefficient alpha paper.

q: Cronbach Meehl 1955 Construct validity in psychological tests Psychological Bulletin
why: Where construct validity was defined.

q: Campbell Fiske 1959 Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix
why: Introduced convergent and discriminant validity.

q: Messick 1995 Validity of psychological assessment: validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning
why: The unified view of validity as evidence for an interpretation — the basis of the modern standards.

q: Fornell Larcker 1981 Evaluating structural equation models with unobservable variables and measurement error Journal of Marketing Research
why: Source of average variance extracted (AVE) and the Fornell–Larcker discriminant-validity criterion.
Introduces the HTMT ratio and shows why Fornell–Larcker often misses discriminant-validity problems.
A critique of how Cronbach's alpha is misused and misread.
Why and how to report omega and other reliability coefficients instead of alpha alone.

q: Tavakol Dennick 2011 Making sense of Cronbach's alpha International Journal of Medical Education
why: A short, readable explanation of what alpha does and does not tell you.

q: Polit Beck Owen 2007 Is the CVI an acceptable indicator of content validity? Appraisal and recommendations
why: How to compute and interpret item- and scale-level content validity indices from expert ratings.
The content validity ratio (CVR) for expert panels.

q: MacKenzie Podsakoff Jarvis 2005 The problem of measurement model misspecification in behavioral and organizational research and some recommended solutions
why: Reflective versus formative indicators, and the bias from getting this wrong.

q: Shrout Fleiss 1979 Intraclass correlations: uses in assessing rater reliability Psychological Bulletin
why: Which intraclass correlation to use for test–retest and inter-rater reliability.

q: Cohen 1960 A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales Educational and Psychological Measurement
why: The original kappa statistic for inter-rater reliability.

q: Bound Krueger 1991 The extent of measurement error in longitudinal earnings data: do two wrongs make a right
why: Measures reporting error in survey earnings against administrative records — reliability in economics data.

q: Morgan 1996 Focus groups Annual Review of Sociology
why: What focus groups are good for, how to run them, and how they combine with surveys.

q: Kallio Pietila Johnson Kangasniemi 2016 Systematic methodological review: developing a framework for a qualitative semi-structured interview guide
why: A five-phase framework for building a semi-structured interview guide.

q: Guest Bunce Johnson 2006 How many interviews are enough? An experiment with data saturation and variability
why: Evidence on when interview data reach saturation.

q: Malterud Siersma Guassora 2016 Sample size in qualitative interview studies: guided by information power
why: Justifying the number of interviews with 'information power' rather than saturation alone.

q: Braun Clarke 2006 Using thematic analysis in psychology Qualitative Research in Psychology
why: The six-phase thematic analysis procedure for interview and FGD data.
Documentation of the Penn World Table — how to read and cite a major secondary macro dataset.

q: Johnson Larson Papageorgiou Subramanian 2013 Is newer better? Penn World Table revisions and their impact on growth estimates
why: Shows that dataset revisions can change results — why you must report the exact data version.

q: Deaton 2005 Measuring poverty in a growing world (or measuring growth in a poor world)
why: Why national accounts and household surveys disagree — a lesson in choosing a data source.

q: Einav Levin 2014 Economics in the age of big data Science
why: New administrative and private-sector data sources and what they offer economic research.
The tidy-data principles: one variable per column, one observation per row.
Practical rules for organising data in spreadsheets before analysis.
A framework for screening, diagnosing and editing data abnormalities.

q: Schafer Graham 2002 Missing data: our view of the state of the art Psychological Methods
why: Missing-data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and modern handling methods.

q: Leys Ley Klein Bernard Licata 2013 Detecting outliers: do not use standard deviation around the mean, use absolute deviation around the median
why: A robust rule for flagging outliers during cleaning.
The ASA statement on p-values — how to report and interpret significance in your results chapter.
